This chapter models a firm that overreports its materials to lower the sales tax it owes. The firm credits the tax paid on its purchases against the tax it owes on its sales, so every peso of fictitious materials lowers its tax bill by the rate on purchases. The chance of being caught and the resources that concealment takes hold it back. Colombian manufacturers faced one rate on their sales and another on their purchases (@sec-setting-incentive): in 56 percent of firm-years the two rates differ by more than one percentage point. I therefore let the two rates differ.

The second rate fits the model to the setting; the approach does not need it. When the two rates coincide, the model reduces to a single-tax model, which @sec-app-single-tax presents. In both models only the rate on purchases enters the decision to overreport, and the test and the deconvolution of @sec-testing and @sec-deconvolution apply unchanged. The second rate changes a single object: the materials share that identifies the output elasticity of materials is measured net of sales taxes rather than gross (@eq-share-net).

## Setup

A firm $i$ in year $t$ produces output with capital $K_{it}$, labour $L_{it}$, and materials $M_{it}$,
$$
Y_{it}=K_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it}+\varepsilon_{it}),
$$ {#eq-pf}
where $\omega_{it}$ is productivity, known to the firm when it chooses its inputs, and $\varepsilon_{it}$ is measurement error in output, with $\mathbb{E}[\varepsilon_{it}]=0$. Because $\varepsilon_{it}$ is an error in the record of output, not a shock to production, the firm's decisions depend on true output, $K_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it})$, and productivity is $\exp(\omega_{it})$. In @Gandhi2020, by contrast, $\varepsilon_{it}$ is a shock to output that the firm does not know when it chooses its inputs. I follow the production-function literature in treating materials as the flexible input, and capital and labour as predetermined or dynamic.

The firm sells its output at price $P_t$ and owes sales tax at rate $\tau_S$ on its sales. It buys materials at price $\rho_t$ and credits the tax paid on them, at rate $\tau_P$, against the tax it owes; when the credit exceeds the tax owed, as for firms exempt from the tax on their sales, the tax authority refunds the difference. The two rates vary across firms and years, because firms sell and buy goods taxed at different rates. The firm claims the credit on reported purchases, $M^*_{it}=M_{it}+e_{it}$, where $e_{it}\ge0$ denotes overreported materials. Capital goods and labour carry no credit (@sec-setting-incentive), so the firm overreports only materials.

Overreporting carries two costs. First, following @Allingham1972, the tax authority audits the firm with probability $q(e_{it})$, which increases with overreporting, with $q(0)=0$, and an audit always uncovers the overreported materials. A firm that is caught repays the credit claimed on $e_{it}$ plus a fine, a multiple $\phi$ of that credit. Second, concealment diverts resources, such as the manager's time, from production; $\kappa_{it}(e_{it},\omega_{it})$ denotes this cost of evasion, which increases in $e_{it}$. Neither the detection probability nor the cost of evasion depends on true materials, so the firm decides how much to overreport separately from how much material to use.

The firm chooses its inputs and overreporting to maximize expected profit,
$$
\begin{aligned}
  \max_{K,L,M,e}\;\mathbb{E}[\pi_{it}] = \;&(1-\tau_S)P_tK_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it})-(1-\tau_P)\rho_tM_{it}-r_tK_{it}-w_tL_{it}\\
  &+\tau_P\rho_te_{it}\big[1-(1+\phi)q(e_{it})\big]-\kappa_{it}(e_{it},\omega_{it}).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-profit}
The first term is revenue net of the tax on sales; the second, the cost of true materials net of the credit on them; the third and fourth, the rental cost of capital and the wage bill. The fifth term is the credit on overreported materials that the firm expects to keep, net of the expected repayment and fine, and the last is the cost of evasion.

@eq-profit nests the single-tax model. With $\tau_S=\tau_P=\tau$, the first two terms become $(1-\tau)\big(P_tK_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta}\exp(\omega_{it})-\rho_tM_{it}\big)$ and the credit on overreported materials becomes $\tau\rho_te_{it}\big[1-(1+\phi)q(e_{it})\big]$. This is the single-tax profit of @sec-app-single-tax.

## First-order conditions

The firm uses materials until their marginal revenue, net of the tax on sales, equals their price, net of the credit:
$$
(1-\tau_S)P_t\,\beta K_{it}^{\alpha_K}L_{it}^{\alpha_L}M_{it}^{\beta-1}\exp(\omega_{it})=(1-\tau_P)\rho_t.
$$ {#eq-foc-m}
Overreporting does not enter @eq-foc-m, because the credit on $e_{it}$ does not depend on true materials. The two rates enter only through the ratio $(1-\tau_P)/(1-\tau_S)$: when the rate on purchases exceeds the rate on sales, the credit lowers the price of materials relative to output, and the firm uses more of them.

Multiplying @eq-foc-m by $M_{it}$ and dividing by measured output, $P_tY_{it}$, gives the log share of materials in output, net of sales taxes:
$$
\ln\left(\frac{(1-\tau_P)\rho_tM_{it}}{(1-\tau_S)P_tY_{it}}\right)=\ln\beta-\varepsilon_{it}.
$$ {#eq-share-net}
With a single rate, the tax terms cancel and the gross share, $\rho_tM_{it}/P_tY_{it}$, satisfies the same equation. @sec-testing builds on @eq-share-net to identify $\beta$.^[The two shares differ little in the data. The log ratio $\ln\big((1-\tau_S)/(1-\tau_P)\big)$ has a standard deviation of 0.05 across firm-years, against 0.34 for the log gross share.]

The firm overreports until the credit it expects to keep on the marginal peso equals the marginal cost of evasion. For an interior choice,
$$
\tau_P\rho_t\big[1-(1+\phi)\big(q(e_{it})+q'(e_{it})e_{it}\big)\big]=\frac{\partial\kappa_{it}(e_{it},\omega_{it})}{\partial e_{it}}.
$$ {#eq-foc-e}
Only the rate on purchases enters @eq-foc-e, because the tax on sales does not depend on reported materials. A higher rate on purchases raises the credit on every fictitious peso, whether or not the firm is caught, so the firm overreports more. By the implicit function theorem, $\partial e^*_{it}/\partial\tau_P>0$ for any detection probability and cost of evasion that satisfy the second-order condition below.

Some firms choose not to overreport at all. For them, the marginal cost of evasion at zero already exceeds the marginal credit, $\tau_P\rho_t\le\partial\kappa_{it}(0,\omega_{it})/\partial e_{it}$, and @eq-foc-e holds as this inequality. Firms that pay no tax on their purchases ($\tau_P=0$) are always in this group.

Corporations are different. Audited statements and scrutiny by government and markets keep them from overreporting (@sec-setting-jo), so $e_{it}=0$ is a constraint for them, not an outcome of @eq-foc-e. I use them only as the truth-reporting benchmark in @sec-testing.

**Draft note:** no exogenous cost shifter $\delta_C$ for corporations (considered, rejected: can't classify corner firms exogenously; the convex $\kappa$ handles both tails through the interior channel alone).

## Second-order condition

- Profit's Hessian is block-diagonal ($e$ separate from $K,L,M$ since $M\perp e$) and the production function is strictly concave, so the second-order condition reduces to $\partial^2\mathbb{E}[\pi_{it}]/\partial e_{it}^2<0$. With a cost of evasion linear in $e_{it}$ and $\phi=0$, it becomes a restriction on the curvature of the detection probability alone (derivation in @sec-app-soc-model):
$$
-\frac{q''(e_{it})}{q'(e_{it})}\,e_{it}<2
$$ {#eq-soc}
- The detection probability may be concave, but not too concave: its elasticity of $q'$ with respect to $e$ must stay above $-2$. A linear $q$ satisfies the condition everywhere ($q''=0$), as does any convex $q$; a concave $q$ such as $1-e^{-\lambda e}$ satisfies it only for $\lambda e<2$.

## Second-order condition

- Profit's Hessian is block-diagonal ($e$ separate from $K,L,M$ since $M\perp e$) and the production function is strictly concave, so the SOC reduces to one condition: $\partial^2\mathbb{E}[\pi_{it}]/\partial e_{it}^2<0$.
- Simplifies (with $\phi=0$) to a restriction on the curvature of $q$ alone:
$$
-\frac{q''(e_{it})}{q'(e_{it})}e_{it}<2
$$ (label removed)
- **Linear $q$ always satisfies this** ($q''=0$). Convex always satisfies it too. Concave needs "not too concave."

## Detection function: three candidates, one headline

- Define the **log marginal benefit** $h(e)\equiv\ln(\tau\rho_t)+\ln(1-q(e)-q'(e)e)$ (with $\phi=0$); the FOC is $h(e)=\ln(\partial\kappa/\partial e)$. [Keep the symbol $h$ generic here -- it's reused with each functional form substituted in.]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

| | $q(e)$ | SOC | $h(e)-\ln(\tau\rho_t)$ | FOC ceiling |
|:--|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| **Linear (headline)** | $\min\{\lambda e,1\}$ | always holds | $\ln(1-2\lambda e)$ | $\lambda e<\tfrac12$ |
| Concave | $1-e^{-\lambda e}$ | $\lambda e<2$ | $-\lambda e+\ln(1-\lambda e)$ | $\lambda e<1$ |
| Convex | $\min\{(\lambda e)^k,1\}$, $k>1$ | always holds | $\ln(1-(1{+}k)(\lambda e)^k)$ | $\lambda e<(1{+}k)^{-1/k}$ |

- **Linear $q=\min\{\lambda e,1\}$ is the headline specification.** Audit-threshold interpretation: tax authority draws $T\sim U[0,1/\lambda]$, audits if $e\ge T$; $1/\lambda$ = largest overreporting any audit tolerates, mean threshold $1/2\lambda$. At the FOC ceiling the most aggressive evader is caught with probability exactly 50% -- a coin flip.

(draft block)
- Concave (exponential) was tested as a robustness check for a specific estimation problem (extreme-evader leverage in $\hat\lambda$, ch. 6/8) and rejected: only delays the ceiling by a fixed ~2x factor, not enough to matter. Convex was not estimated (would only tighten the ceiling further, the wrong direction for that problem).


- **Report detection probability in relative terms, not absolute.** Without independent audit-rate data, $q$'s absolute level isn't calibratable -- a skeptic can dispute $\hat\lambda$. But under linear $q$, $q(e_A)/q(e_B)=e_A/e_B$ is exactly $\hat\lambda$-invariant, so relative detection risk against a benchmark (e.g. the median evader) is a robust, assumption-light readout of the evasion distribution alone. [(Table with real numbers: ch. 8.)]{.content-visible when-meta="draft"}

## Cost of evasion

- $\kappa_{it}(e_{it},\omega_{it})=e_{it}\exp\{\delta_0-\delta_1\omega_{it}+\delta_2\omega_{it}^2+\psi_{it}\}$ -- linear in $e$ (tractable: gives $e^*$ in closed form under linear $q$), **convex in $\omega$** (minimum at $\omega^*=\delta_1/2\delta_2$).
- Economic rationale for the convexity: more productive firms have more resources to hide evasion in, but the most productive firms also have the best access to *legal* avoidance, so illegal evasion costs them more at the margin -- both tails of the productivity distribution evade less than the middle.
- $\psi_{it}$: idiosyncratic cost shock, the source of evasion heterogeneity beyond what $\omega$ explains.
- Substituting linear $q$ and this $\kappa$ into @eq-foc-e and taking logs:
$$
\psi_{it}=h(e_{it})-\delta_0+\delta_1\omega_{it}-\delta_2\omega_{it}^2,\qquad h(e_{it})=\ln(\tau\rho_t)+\ln(1-2\lambda e_{it})
$$ (label removed)
  This is the equation every stage-2 estimator (ch. 6, 8) is built from.
- $q$ and $\kappa$ are not separately identified without independent audit data; functional-form assumptions here are what let estimation reproduce the observed evasion-by-productivity pattern (ch. 7's motivating fact, @Carrillo2022).
